title: Switching Into Tech Without Starting From Zero
summary: Moving into tech, or to a new role inside it, comes with an awkward middle. What research says about feeling like a fraud, and why trying comes before deciding.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
It's 11 p.m. You've got a laptop, a notebook and far too many tabs open. One explains HTTP, one explains Git, and one promises that learning to code is easy if you follow ten simple steps, which doesn't feel true at this hour. You're learning technology, sure. You're also slowly trading one professional identity for another, and that's the harder part.

"Moving into tech" covers a lot of ground: someone leaving another career for software, a tester becoming a developer, a backend engineer moving toward AI, a developer stepping up to tech lead. From the outside, each one is a tidy label. From the inside, your old fluency fades before the new one shows up.

The awkward middle

The middle stage is uncomfortable because it asks capable people to be beginners again. You used to be the one who knew how things worked. Now a simple command fails, a code review uses words you've never heard, and a diagram assumes things everyone else seems to know. Losing fluency feels personal, even though it's exactly what learning a new field looks like.

If that comes with a voice saying you're a fraud and someone will find out, you have plenty of company. A 2020 review of 62 studies with 14,161 participants found impostor feelings in anywhere from 9% to 82% of people, depending on the screening tool and cutoff, in men and women alike and from teenagers to late-career professionals (Bravata et al., Journal of General Internal Medicine). The range is wide because the measuring is messy. By definition, though, impostor syndrome describes high achievers who can't take in their own success, so the feeling says very little about whether you belong. The same review found no published studies testing treatments. One practical habit helps anyway: keep a list of things you couldn't do three months ago.

You're not starting from zero

You bring plenty from your last chapter: talking to customers, domain knowledge, writing, running a meeting, patience with messy processes, keeping your head in a crisis. Tech has its own vocabulary, but it still runs on people, trade-offs and clear thinking. A former accountant who knows reconciliation inside out will catch bugs in a payment flow that a fresh CS grad walks right past. A former teacher already knows how to explain hard things simply, which is half of writing good docs.

My own path has a few turns in it: front-end at a real-estate startup in 2018, Java at an outsourcing company in 2019 (the same year I finished a 240-hour software testing course), four years of full-stack work at a product startup, then Zalo PC in 2024 and my first Lead title in 2025. Every turn came with a new vocabulary to learn.

Try first, decide later

Herminia Ibarra studied people in the middle of career changes and saw many of them follow the classic advice (figure out what you want, then act on it) and stay stuck for months or even years. Her conclusion: doing comes first, knowing second. Most people built their new working identity on the side at first, through weekend projects and extra work, a practice she calls crafting experiments. She also writes that most career transitions take about three years and rarely move in a straight line (How to Stay Stuck in the Wrong Career).

When you're moving into or within tech, an experiment can be tiny: an app that reads a file, calls an API, saves a record and shows a page. One full loop like that teaches more than a huge unfinished dream. You find out where setup hurts, where your understanding is thin, what deploying changes and how a user actually experiences the thing. Side projects are a great home for these experiments (more in What a Small Side Project Teaches You). Inside your current job, volunteer for the work next door: write the test plan, fix a small bug, sit in on the design review.

A few practice habits that work: read a bit of code every day, keep notes in your own words, ask one clear question instead of sitting on ten vague doubts, and look at old mistakes without letting them define you. Progress usually shows up first as fewer repeated mistakes. The confidence arrives later, sometimes much later.

Be honest about money and time

Comparison is a cost nobody mentions. Online, everyone seems faster. Coworkers already speak in shorthand. Job posts list a stack as long as a grocery receipt. Yet most people in tech are switching in smaller ways all the time: new frameworks, new domains, new tools. Learning isn't the entrance exam for this field. It's most of the job.

Money and status deserve honesty too. A switch might need savings, family support or a slower path than the success stories suggest. Not everyone can quit and study full time. Lots of people learn between shifts, after the kids are asleep or over lunch. Ibarra's three years is a good number to remember here: if it feels slow, you may be right on schedule.

Changing fields is a lot like moving to a new city. At first every street name is foreign. Then a few routes start to feel familiar. One day you give someone directions and realize you've stopped translating the signs in your head.

Try this week

  • Write down three skills from your previous role and one place each shows up in tech work.
  • Build one full loop: read data, call an API, store it, show it. Ugly is fine.
  • Start a "couldn't do this three months ago" list and add a line every Friday.
  • When you've been stuck for an hour, ask one clear question in your team channel before starting a second hour alone.
  • Find someone who made the same switch and ask how long it really took.

faqs.q: How long does a career change into tech take?
faqs.a: It depends a lot on where you start, your savings and how much time you have. Herminia Ibarra, who studied people changing careers, writes that most career transitions take about three years and rarely move in a straight line. A slow first year is normal.

faqs.q: Is impostor syndrome normal when switching into tech?
faqs.a: Very common. A 2020 review of 62 studies found impostor feelings in 9% to 82% of participants depending on how they were measured, across genders and career stages. Impostor syndrome describes people who can't take in their own real success, so keep concrete evidence of your progress instead of trusting the feeling.

faqs.q: Should I quit my job to learn to code?
faqs.a: Only if your savings and situation allow it. Ibarra found that most people who changed careers started with experiments on the side, such as weekend projects or extra assignments, before making the leap. Learning alongside your current job is slower but much less risky.
